summary: Describes mesh-enhanced SLP, which adds to the Service Location Protocol a set of Directory Agents that peer with each other in shared scopes and swap new service registrations. This improves reliability and scalability of finding services on a network. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3528 improves the Service Location Protocol by letting the directory agents that serve the same scope talk to each other in a fully meshed group. A service that registers with one of them is passed on to the others, so a service agent no longer has to register with every directory agent on the network.

questions: service location protocol directory agent peering
how do directory agents share services
is mslp backward compatible with slp
subtitle: Directory Agents that peer with each other in fully meshed groups and share new service registrations.

tldr.problem: In the Service Location Protocol version 2, a service agent that wants to be found must register with every directory agent in its scope, and must re-register whenever a directory agent appears or reboots.
tldr.mechanism: mSLP makes the directory agents in a scope peer with each other in a full mesh, and adds an extension that carries a version timestamp and an accept identifier so registrations can be propagated and ordered correctly.
tldr.outcome: The memo says mSLP is backward compatible with SLP version 2 and can be deployed incrementally, so existing peers keep working. It is an Experimental document.

today: RFC 3528 is an Experimental document, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo presents mSLP as a lightweight enhancement to the Service Location Protocol that is backward compatible with version 2 and can be deployed incrementally, rather than as a replacement for it.

sections.title: Introduction and Compatibility
sections.content:
In the Service Location Protocol version 2, Directory Agents accept service registrations from Service Agents and answer queries from User Agents. They improve the performance and scalability of SLPv2, and the use of scopes improves scalability further. A Directory Agent can serve multiple scopes, and a scope can be served by multiple Directory Agents. The memo addresses the question this leaves open: when several Directory Agents serve the same scope, how should they interact with each other?

The answer is a scope-based fully meshed peering architecture. For each scope, all the Directory Agents serving that scope form a fully meshed peer relationship, similar to the way internal BGP peers are related. Peer Directory Agents exchange new service registrations in shared scopes through anti-entropy and through direct forwarding.

mSLP is designed as a lightweight enhancement to SLPv2 and is backward compatible with it. It defines two enhanced entities, a Mesh-enhanced Directory Agent and a Mesh-enhanced Service Agent, and they can be deployed incrementally. An enhanced entity supports the extended operations without affecting its original functionality as defined in RFC 2608, and for simplicity an enhanced entity works as a non-enhanced entity when it talks to a non-enhanced one.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo answers an open question in the Service Location Protocol: when several directory agents serve the same scope, they need to agree. The answer is to have them peer with each other. The change is small enough that a network can adopt it one machine at a time.

sections.title: The Scope-Based Fully-Meshed Peer Architecture
sections.content:
For each scope, all the Mesh-enhanced Directory Agents serving that scope form a fully meshed peer relationship. A single peering connection between two peers carries all the service registrations in their shared scopes. The architecture improves the consistency among peer Directory Agents, because inconsistent states are reconciled automatically, and it lets a newly booted or rebooted agent catch up on all new registrations at once from its peers, purely through Directory Agent interaction and without involving Service Agents.

It also simplifies Service Agent registrations. In SLPv2 a Service Agent must discover and register with all existing Directory Agents in its scopes, and re-register when new ones are discovered or old ones are found to have rebooted. In mSLP, a Mesh-enhanced Service Agent only needs to discover and register with a sufficient number of them, such that the union of their scopes covers its own scopes, because the registrations are then propagated automatically.

The memo also sets out the scaling advantage. Consider a scope with N Service Agents and M Directory Agents, where N is greater than M and M is at least two. Both mSLP and SLPv2 need the same number of SLP messages to distribute the registrations, but the agents doing the distribution differ: in SLPv2 they are all N Service Agents, and in mSLP they are only the M Directory Agents. The number of TCP connections needed also differs. SLPv2 needs N times M, because each Service Agent connects to each Directory Agent, while mSLP needs N plus M times (M minus 1) divided by two, because each Service Agent connects to one Directory Agent and the registrations then travel through the mesh. For N of 100 and M of 10, SLPv2 needs 1000 TCP connections and mSLP needs 145.

The memo is candid about the limit this puts on the design. Because the topology is a full mesh, chosen mainly for simplicity and reliability, it cannot scale to a large number of agents in a single mesh; in general mSLP applies when the number of agents in a mesh is on the order of tens or below. The way out is to split a scope into finer scopes, so a scope x with too many agents becomes x-1 and x-2, each with its own smaller full mesh, and a registration for scope x must then be registered under both.
sections.plainLanguage: Directory agents in the same scope are linked to each other, all to all. A service that registers with one is passed to the rest, which saves each service agent from registering everywhere. The design does not scale to very large groups, so the memo says to split a busy scope into smaller ones.

sections.title: Managing Peer Relationships
sections.content:
An agent learns about new peers through static configuration, DHCP, or the multicast and unicast DAAdvert message, and in every case it MUST obtain a peer's DAAdvert before establishing a peer relationship with that peer. It then opens a peering connection if one does not already exist and sends its own DAAdvert over it. An agent can tell that a connection was initiated by the peer, because the peer's DAAdvert arrives on that connection. Normally one connection is set up between two peers, but a pair can end up with two if both initiate at nearly the same moment, so an agent that notices this SHOULD check whether it opened the other one and, if it has a lower-numbered IP address, SHOULD terminate the connection it opened.

Once the connection exists, the two peers exchange information about their existing peers by forwarding those peers' DAAdverts over the connection. An agent forwards a third party's DAAdvert to a new peer when that third party shares scopes with the new peer and is either an active peer of the first agent or an accept DA for registrations the first agent currently holds. All the DAAdverts can travel as one TCP stream.

To detect failures, the peers use a heart-beat: an agent sends its DAAdvert to its peers every CONFIG_DA_KEEPALIVE seconds, and the timeout for that message is CONFIG_DA_TIMEOUT seconds. An agent SHOULD tear down a peer relationship when the peer closes the peering connection, when it receives a DAAdvert multicast from the peer with a DA stateless boot timestamp of zero, meaning the peer is going to shut down, or when it has not received the peer's DAAdvert for more than CONFIG_DA_TIMEOUT seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Agents find each other, open a connection, and then tell each other about the other agents they know. Each sends a short advertisement on a timer so the others notice if one goes away, and close the relationship when it does.

sections.title: Registration Propagation Control
sections.content:
When an agent accepts a registration update from a Service Agent, it assigns the update a unique accept ID, which has two parts: the URL of the accepting agent and an accept timestamp. The accept timestamp is a 64-bit integer counting elapsed microseconds since 00:00 UTC on January 1, 1900, and all accept timestamps assigned by the same agent MUST be monotonically increasing. A registration state carries the same accept ID as the latest update applied to it. An agent MUST propagate registrations in increasing order of their accept IDs, so registrations from the same accepting agent travel in the order they were accepted, while registrations from different accepting agents may travel in any order.

Arrival timestamps cannot settle which version of a registration is newer, because a registration may reach one agent before a newer version of it reaches another. mSLP therefore uses version timestamps. When a Mesh-enhanced Service Agent sends a registration update, it assigns a version timestamp, again a 64-bit integer counting microseconds since the same epoch, and all version timestamps assigned by the same agent MUST be monotonically increasing. Because mSLP assumes each registration is updated by only one Service Agent, an agent does not need to compare version timestamps from different Service Agents. It installs an update if the update has a newer version timestamp, or if the update does not carry the Mesh Forwarding extension, which is the case for a non-enhanced Service Agent.

The Mesh Forwarding extension carries the version timestamp and an accept ID entry, and it is used with a Srv(De)Reg message, but only with a fresh registration or a complete deregistration. It defines two forwarding IDs. RqstFwd is used by a Service Agent, with an accept timestamp of zero, to ask the accepting agent explicitly to forward the message. Fwded is used by an accepting agent in each message it sends to another agent, either forwarding a message it received from a Service Agent or propagating a registration state from its own database. A separate summary vector records, for each accept DA the agent has heard from, the latest accept timestamp, which tells the agent how far it has caught up with each of them. When a deregistration arrives with the Mesh Forwarding extension, the agent SHOULD keep the registration in its database and mark it as deleted, so it does not appear in any query reply and an earlier registration cannot bring it back.
sections.plainLanguage: Each registration carries two clocks: one that says when the agent that accepted it saw it, and one that says which version it is. Those let the agents agree on an order and stop an older version from overwriting a newer one, even when the messages arrive out of order.

sections.title: Anti-Entropy and Direct Forwarding
sections.content:
Anti-entropy is used to exchange initial registration states when two peers recognize each other for the first time, and to update new registration states after failures. An agent sends an Anti-entropy Request, which carries an anti-entropy type and a list of accept ID entries. The type is either selective, in which case only registration states with an accept ID greater than any accept ID named in the message are requested, or complete, in which case all states with a greater accept ID are requested, together with every state whose accept DA is not named in the message at all.

On receiving an Anti-entropy Request, the agent sends the requested new registration states in increasing order of their accept IDs, and at least a Service Acknowledgment message to say that the request has been processed. A new state is sent as a fresh registration with its remaining lifetime, and a newly deregistered state is propagated as a deregistration. Several such messages can travel as one TCP stream.

After sending all the new registration states it accepted itself to a peer through anti-entropy, an agent directly forwards newly received registration updates from Service Agents to that peer until a failure occurs. In a direct forward the forwarding ID is Fwded and the accept timestamp is the arrival timestamp at the forwarding agent. Direct forwarding is asynchronous: the forwarding agent can send a Service Acknowledgment to the Service Agent before it forwards the message to its peers. Direct forwarding goes one hop only, from the accepting agent to all of that agent's peers that are in the registration scopes.

The memo also states when acknowledgments are sent. A Directory Agent must reply with a Service Acknowledgment to a registration or deregistration received from a Service Agent, but a Mesh-enhanced agent should not reply to one received from a peer, because peers exchange these messages over reliable peering connections. It must reply to an Anti-entropy Request.
sections.plainLanguage: Two mechanisms move registrations around. Anti-entropy is a catch-up: an agent asks a peer for everything it is missing. Direct forwarding is a relay: a message received from a service agent is passed straight on to the peers, one hop only.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
mSLP uses the standard SLPv2 authentication, and the memo adds three recommendations about where it should be applied.

First, an agent SHOULD authenticate other agents before setting up a peer relationship with them, so that a malicious agent cannot join the mesh. Second, because a successful attack on one agent can affect every agent in the mesh, an agent SHOULD authenticate Service Agents before accepting and forwarding their registration messages, so that service registrations cannot be modified or removed illegitimately. Third, because a Service Agent depends on the agent it registers with to forward its messages, it SHOULD authenticate that agent, to avoid using a malicious one.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo uses the authentication already in the Service Location Protocol, and says where it must be applied: between directory agents that peer, between directory agents and the service agents that register with them, and between a service agent and the directory agent it relies on.
